notes.meaning: Israel arrives in the Wilderness of Zin and camps at Kadesh during the first month of the fortieth year of their journey. Miriam, the older sister of Moses and Aaron who had helped lead the people, dies and is buried there. Her death shows that the older generation was passing away, just as the Lord had promised.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic writers saw Miriam as a picture of the Virgin Mary, pointing to her unmarried life and her leadership among the women of Israel.

notes.meaning: The community runs out of water at Kadesh, creating a serious crisis in the dry desert. Instead of turning to the Lord in prayer, the people crowd together in anger against Moses and Aaron. This water shortage tested whether the younger generation had learned to trust God better than their parents did.

The Israelites bring a bitter, formal complaint against Moses. In their panic, they say they would rather have died suddenly in God's earlier judgments than face thirst in the wilderness. Their anger shows that they had quickly adopted the same rebellious attitude as their parents.

The crowd blames Moses and Aaron for leading them into the desert to let their families and animals perish. They speak as if the Lord's chosen servants were deliberately trying to kill them. This unfair accusation repeated the exact words of the previous generation decades before.

The people complain about the harshness of the desert, noting that it has no seed, figs, grapevines, pomegranates, or water. They focus entirely on what they do not have instead of thanking God for the manna that fed them every day. In their discontent, they forget their former slavery in Egypt and belittle the land God promised them.

Moses and Aaron leave the angry assembly and go to the door of the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God met with His people. They fall facedown to seek God's protection and guidance for the rebellious camp. The Lord answers by showing His radiant glory, calming the crisis and reassuring His servants.

The Lord tells Moses to take his staff and gather the whole congregation together with Aaron. Instead of hitting anything, they are simply to speak to the rock before everyone's eyes so it will release water. God promises to bring out enough water to satisfy the thirst of all the people and their animals.

Moses goes into the sanctuary and takes the staff from the Lord's presence, just as he was told. This was the famous rod used during the plagues of Egypt and the crossing of the Red Sea. Holding it served to remind both the leaders and the people of God's mighty past deliverances.

Moses and Aaron assemble the people before the rock, but Moses speaks out of deep frustration and anger. He scolds the crowd as rebels and asks if he and Aaron must bring water out of the rock for them. By saying 'must we,' Moses speaks rashly and fails to give God all the credit for the miracle.

Moses raises his hand and hits the rock twice with his staff instead of speaking to it. Even though His servant acted in hot temper, God remains merciful and causes a river of water to gush out. The vast crowd and all their livestock receive the water they urgently needed.

The Lord disciplines Moses and Aaron because their angry words and actions failed to trust Him and honor Him as holy in the eyes of Israel. Because of this public failure, God announces that neither of them will lead the nation into the promised land. God holds His leaders to a strict standard because they represent His character to the world.

differ.view: Many evangelicals teach that Moses ruined a sacred picture of Christ, who was struck once on the cross and only needs to be spoken to in prayer afterward.
Some Baptists teach that the core sin was not striking the rock, but doubting in the heart whether God was truly willing to show mercy to such rebels.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching often describes this failure as a momentary lapse or weakness in faith rather than a total loss of trust, with some church fathers viewing the two blows as a symbol of the cross.

notes.meaning: The water is named Meribah, which means 'strife' or 'quarreling,' because Israel argued with the Lord there. Even in the middle of their complaints and Moses' error, God proved that He is holy by providing for the crowd and judging sin. The name served as a warning for future generations not to test God.

Moses sends diplomats from Kadesh to the king of Edom to ask for safe passage through his territory. He addresses the king as a brother because the Edomites descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob. He appeals to this family bond and reminds Edom of the terrible struggles Israel had endured.

The messengers explain how Israel suffered mistreatment as slaves in Egypt for generations. When they cried out, the Lord answered their prayers and sent His angel to rescue them and guide them to Edom's border. Moses shares this rescue story to show that God is on Israel's side and deserves Edom's respect.

Israel politely requests permission to walk straight through Edom's land. They promise not to damage grain fields or vineyards, and they agree not to take well water without permission. They offer to stay strictly on the King's Highway, the main public trade route, until they exit the country.

The king of Edom gives a sharp and hostile refusal to Israel's polite request. He warns them that if they set foot in his land, he will march out to attack them with an army. This harsh answer reflected the old jealousy that Esau held against Jacob.

The Israelite messengers try once more to reassure the king. They repeat that they will only walk on the main road and offer to pay full price for any water used by the people or their herds. They emphasize that they are peaceful travelers who mean no harm.

Edom refuses a second time and gathers a powerful, heavily armed force along the border to block the passage. Rather than waging war against their relatives, Israel obeys God's boundaries and turns away to find another route. This forced the nation to take a far longer and harder road around Edom.

The entire assembly packs up their camp and journeys from Kadesh to Mount Hor. This prominent mountain sat right along the border of the land of Edom. It becomes the solemn location where Aaron finishes his earthly life.

At Mount Hor, the Lord tells Moses and Aaron that the time has come for Aaron to die and be gathered to his ancestors. Aaron is forbidden from entering the promised land because he joined in disobeying God's command at the waters of Meribah. Even so, God treats His aged high priest with great dignity and peace in his final hours.

God commands Moses to lead Aaron and his son Eleazar up to the top of Mount Hor. There, Moses must take off Aaron's sacred priestly robes and place them onto Eleazar. This public ceremony showed that while the individual priest dies, the priesthood itself continues without interruption.

Moses obeys the Lord, and the three leaders climb the mountain in full view of the whole camp. After Moses transfers the holy vestments to Eleazar, Aaron dies peacefully on the mountain peak. Moses and the new high priest then descend the mountain to rejoin the congregation.

The entire nation realizes that Aaron has passed away when they see Eleazar wearing the high priest's garments. The people spend thirty full days in deep national mourning to honor Aaron's long service. Though they had often grumbled against him in life, they recognized his great worth after he was gone.
